neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and fully oriented. Anxious about his weakness.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral facial weakness — forehead sparing absent (symmetric facial diplegia; upper and lower face involved). Dysarthria noted. Difficulty closing eyes fully bilaterally. All other cranial nerves intact.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral lower extremity weakness: hip flexion 4/5, knee extension 4/5, ankle dorsiflexion 3/5 bilaterally. Upper extremity: shoulder abduction 4/5, wrist extension 4/5, grip 4/5 bilaterally. Increased fatigue with sustained effort.
neurological_exam.sensory: Bilateral distal lower extremity paresthesias (glove-and-stocking distribution). Mild reduction in vibration at bilateral ankles.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Absent deep tendon reflexes throughout: areflexia at bilateral biceps, triceps, brachioradialis, patellar, and Achilles. This is the most alarming finding.
neurological_exam.coordination: Cannot assess reliably due to weakness.
neurological_exam.gait: Cannot stand without assistance. Too weak to attempt tandem gait.
neurological_exam.additional: Respiratory: Forced vital capacity (FVC) measured at bedside: 2.2 L (predicted 3.8 L — 58% of predicted). NIF: -28 cmH2O. These values are concerning but not yet at intubation threshold.

patient.chief_complaint: Ten-day progressive bilateral leg weakness, paresthesias, and facial diplegia with areflexia.
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. H. is a 50-year-old man presenting to the emergency department with a 10-day history of progressive neurological symptoms. Approximately 3 weeks ago, he had a mild upper respiratory illness that resolved after 5 days. One week after recovery, he began noticing tingling in both feet. Over the following days, the tingling ascended to his knees and he developed progressive leg weakness — initially difficulty climbing stairs, then difficulty rising from a chair. By day 7, he noticed bilateral facial weakness and slurred speech. He presents today unable to walk without support. He has also noted dysphagia for thin liquids over the past 2 days and reports that his voice sounds 'nasal.' His wife noticed bilateral facial drooping which is now symmetric. He denies bladder dysfunction. He denies neck stiffness or fever. He has no history of tick exposure, recent travel, or toxin exposure. His symptoms have been progressive throughout with no fluctuation or improvement.

specialized_test.impression: This is an ABNORMAL nerve conduction study. 1. Markedly prolonged distal motor latencies and reduced conduction velocities in bilateral median and peroneal motor nerves. 2. Absent sural sensory nerve action potentials bilaterally. 3. Absent F-waves bilaterally in median and peroneal nerves, indicating proximal conduction failure. 4. Absent H-reflex bilaterally. Electrophysiological pattern is consistent with a demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. Clinical correlation recommended.

differential.key_features: MRI shows nerve root enhancement but no cord signal change; no sensory level; no UMN signs; no sphincter dysfunction
Onset 10 days — too acute for CIDP (>8 weeks required); no relapsing-remitting course
Sensory symptoms present in GBS; no descending pattern; no food exposure; NCS shows demyelinating not normal pattern
No UMN signs; areflexia rather than hyperreflexia; MRI shows no compression

optimal_actions.action: Order urgent labs including Campylobacter serology and inflammatory markers
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Campylobacter IgM positive; mild leukocytosis; elevated CRP/ESR
Demyelinating pattern: prolonged DML, reduced CV, absent F-waves, absent SNAPs
FVC approaching intubation threshold — close monitoring required
Albumino-cytologic dissociation — elevated protein with normal cells
Sinus tachycardia; autonomic dysrhythmias on monitoring
Anti-GM1 and anti-GD1a IgG positive — motor-predominant post-Campylobacter
Cauda equina nerve root enhancement — confirms inflammatory polyradiculopathy

critical_actions: Admit to monitored unit (ICU or step-down) — FVC and NIF approaching intubation thresholds
Serial respiratory monitoring every 4-6 hours (FVC, NIF, ABG)
Initiate IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days (or plasmapheresis as alternative)
Continuous cardiac telemetry — autonomic dysrhythmias are common and potentially dangerous
DVT prophylaxis — immobilized patient at high VTE risk
contraindicated_actions: Corticosteroids — not effective in GBS and may worsen outcome
Combining IVIG and plasmapheresis — no additive benefit; start with one
Sedating medications — risk of respiratory failure in patient with reduced FVC
NSAIDs — avoid in setting of autonomic instability
key_reasoning_points: Bilateral facial diplegia + ascending weakness + areflexia + antecedent C. jejuni infection = classic GBS; facial diplegia in 50% of GBS
CSF protein only borderline elevated at 10 days — albumino-cytologic dissociation is not always maximal at presentation; may peak at 2-4 weeks
Anti-GM1/GD1a IgG positivity in post-Campylobacter GBS predicts risk of axonal variant (AMAN) — repeat NCS in 1-2 weeks
Respiratory monitoring is life-critical — 20/30% of GBS patients require mechanical ventilation
The '20-30-40 rule': intubate when FVC <20 mL/kg, NIF worse than -30 cmH2O, or VC <40% predicted

red_herrings.data_point: Mild leukocytosis (WBC 11.2 x10^9/L) and elevated CRP/ESR
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggest ongoing active infection or sepsis as the primary cause of symptoms rather than post-infectious autoimmune GBS
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Mild leukocytosis and inflammatory markers reflect the preceding Campylobacter jejuni infection and are expected in GBS 10 days after antecedent illness; they do not indicate active systemic infection driving the neurological syndrome
